title: Critical minerals need secure supply chains – increasingly that depends on responsible production
gist: Recorded human rights abuses tied to transition minerals jumped 73% between 2024 and 2025, with seven in ten implicated mines linked to listed companies and over half of global critical minerals sitting under or near Indigenous lands. Community protest is now interrupting, suspending and cancelling mining projects worldwide, while liability spreads downstream to tech buyers and even to the standards bodies that certify them. The twist: producer states such as the DRC are picking up the responsible-business toolkit built in the 2000s and using it as leverage against great-power competition for supply.

themes.theme: Social risk is now a production risk in transition minerals

insights.claim: The Business and Human Rights Centre recorded a 73% increase in human rights abuses linked to transition minerals between 2024 and 2025.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A doubling-in-two-years trajectory in recorded abuse cases is a leading indicator of litigation, permit delay and offtake disruption across the battery-metals complex.
insights.quote: The Business and Human Rights Centre recorded a 73% increase in human rights abuses linked to transition minerals between 2024 to 2025.
insights.locator: Global trade wars, geo-economic competition

insights.claim: Seven in ten mines implicated in recorded transition-minerals human rights abuses were tied to listed companies, meaning the exposure sits in public equity rather than in private or informal operators.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Investors cannot assume abuse risk is confined to unlisted artisanal supply; screen listed miners' site-level incident records, not just their policy disclosures.
insights.quote: Seven in ten implicated mines were tied to listed companies.
insights.locator: Seven in ten implicated mines

insights.claim: More than half of critical minerals worldwide are located under or in close proximity to Indigenous lands, making Indigenous consent a structural gating factor on future supply.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Resource-to-production conversion rates should be discounted for consent risk; projects with genuine FPIC processes deserve a valuation premium over paper reserves.
insights.quote: More than half of critical minerals worldwide are located under or near Indigenous lands.
insights.locator: More than half of critical minerals worldwide

insights.claim: Community protests have interrupted production, forced suspension of operations and at times curtailed or cancelled entire mining projects across Africa, South and Southeast Asia, Europe, and North and Latin America, making social opposition a global rather than regional phenomenon.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Model community opposition as a base-rate schedule risk on every greenfield mine, including in OECD jurisdictions, not as an emerging-market-only discount.
insights.quote: community protests have interrupted production, suspend operations and at times even curtailed if not cancelled entire projects in Africa, South and Southeast Asia, Europe and North and Latin America
insights.locator: There is also a strong business case

insights.claim: Global demand for lithium carbonate equivalent rose from roughly 68,000 metric tonnes in 2000 to an estimated 1.5 to 1.8 million tonnes by 2025, a more than twentyfold expansion in market scale.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Supply chains that scale this fast cannot be fully formalised, so due-diligence gaps in lithium and adjacent battery inputs are structural rather than cyclical.
insights.quote: In 2000 global demand for lithium carbonate equivalent was approximately 68,000 metric tonnes. By 2025, industry estimates had risen to 1.5 to 1.8 million tonnes.
insights.locator: The sharp increase in demand for many materials

insights.claim: Rapid increases in minerals market scale are partly filled by artisanal and informal production, which raises the probability of child labour, environmental damage, illegal trading and malign actors entering the supply chain.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Demand spikes mechanically degrade supply-chain provenance quality, so the fastest-growing minerals carry the highest headline and regulatory risk for downstream buyers.
insights.locator: Such rapid increases in market scale

insights.claim: Sharply rising demand for materials increases downstream company exposure to upstream risk factors, transmitting mine-site problems into the balance sheets of manufacturers and technology buyers.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Upstream incidents are now a downstream earnings and legal risk; map tier-2 and tier-3 supplier concentration for auto, electronics and defence names.
insights.quote: The sharp increase in demand for many materials increases downstream company exposure to upstream risk factors.
insights.locator: The sharp increase in demand

themes.theme: Liability is migrating downstream and onto standards bodies

insights.claim: International activists and the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo have filed multiple legal actions against large technology companies over the use of DRC minerals, alleging downstream corporate complicity in human rights abuse and child labour at the point of extraction.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Producer governments themselves are now plaintiffs, which raises settlement risk and diligence cost for electronics and EV supply chains sourcing from the DRC.
insights.quote: International activists and the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have filed multiple legal actions against large tech companies for using DRC minerals in their supply chains
insights.locator: International activists and the government

insights.claim: Legal action is now targeting the standards bodies that validate corporate no-harm claims, including a case involving Tanzanian gold workers that establishes a new focus of liability with potentially wide repercussions.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: If certifiers can be sued, certification pricing, insurance and willingness to audit will tighten, weakening the assurance layer that downstream buyers currently rely on.
insights.quote: including one case involving Tanzanian gold workers that represents a new focus of liability on standards bodies that could have wide repercussions
insights.locator: Legal action is also targeting standards bodies

insights.claim: A structural standoff exists in verification: regulators demand total supply chain assurance while companies are reticent to accept due diligence responsibility beyond their immediate suppliers.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: That gap is the commercial opening for traceability, provenance-verification and assurance providers, and the compliance cost line for buyers who lose the argument.
insights.quote: Verification schemes face a challenge as regulators desire total supply chain assurance, while companies are reticent to accept responsibility for due diligence beyond their immediate suppliers.
insights.locator: Verification schemes face a challenge

insights.claim: Sanctions imposed by Canada, the EU, UK and USA on Russia's oil and diamond businesses after the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine prompted existing mechanisms to verify provenance claims in those markets.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Sanctions enforcement has become the practical driver of provenance infrastructure, so expect the same verification machinery to be extended to other strategic minerals.
insights.locator: Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022

themes.theme: Geopolitics weaponising supply chains against responsibility

insights.claim: Geopolitical instability, rather than economic or financial factors, is the dominant risk to international trade, with scholarly studies and company surveys pointing to political factors as the biggest threat to global commerce as states reassert control over markets.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Political risk premia belong in trade-exposed industrial and commodity valuations as a persistent input, not an episodic shock overlay.
insights.quote: Geopolitical instability is the dominant risk to international trade.
insights.locator: Changing risks

insights.claim: Governments are prioritising minerals supply chains as instruments of geopolitical and economic advantage - to reduce Chinese dominance, to avoid chokepoints, or to disengage from abusive actors - often without considering the ecological and human rights risks this creates in producer states.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: State-driven friend-shoring can raise, not lower, the ESG risk embedded in new supply, so de-risking announcements should not be read as risk reduction at the asset level.
insights.locator: Companies now need to be more aware

insights.claim: Governments must avoid a 'race to the bottom' on responsibility and instead ensure sufficient protection exists for companies to uphold responsible performance and protect the intangible but at times material social licence to operate.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Social licence is treated here as a material asset; its loss shows up as suspended operations, so track community relations as a hard operating metric.
insights.quote: Governments have to avoid the pitfall of a ‘race to the bottom’ on responsibility
insights.locator: Governments have to avoid the pitfall

insights.claim: Contemporary global minerals standards were built in part on the targeted mechanisms developed in the 1980s and 1990s to restrict minerals funding proxy conflicts, giving today's frameworks a conflict-finance rather than purely environmental lineage.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Understanding the conflict-finance origin explains why sanctions and provenance regimes converge on the same verification tooling.
insights.locator: To some extent, global standards were built

themes.theme: The business case for responsible performance

insights.claim: Proponents of responsible-business standards argue that responsible companies enjoy lower capital costs, stronger risk management, better employee retention and more stable long-term financial performance, while critics point to the cost and complexity of conformance.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The claimed payoff is a financing-cost spread, so compare capital costs of high-conformance versus low-conformance miners rather than debating disclosure quality.
insights.quote: responsible companies often enjoy lower capital costs, stronger risk management, better employee retention, and more stable long-term financial performance
insights.locator: Proponents of standards argue

insights.claim: Companies and governments may believe corporate responsibility and accountability have gone out of fashion, but affected communities and environmental and human rights defenders have not accepted that shift, and protests and disruptions continue to mount.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Deregulatory sentiment in capitals does not reduce on-the-ground disruption risk; the divergence creates mispriced operational risk in mining equities.
insights.quote: Companies and governments may think that corporate responsibility and accountability have gone out of fashion. Affected communities and environmental and human rights defenders may not have gotten the memo as protests and disruptions mount.
insights.locator: Companies and governments may think

insights.claim: Conformance with responsible-business standards functions as a shield and robust safeguard against accusations of malfeasance in difficult operating environments, rather than merely as a compliance cost.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Reframe audit and certification spend as legal-defence and insurance expenditure when assessing whether a miner's compliance budget is adequate.
insights.locator: And while critics highlight the cost

themes.theme: Standards are not Western, and China is moving

insights.claim: Business and human rights frameworks are not inherently Western: the UN Global Compact set out responsible business guidelines in 2000, and the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights were unanimously agreed by the UN Human Rights Council in 2011.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
entities: UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights
insights.so_what: Undercuts the argument that dropping these standards is a competitiveness win for non-Western operators; universal buy-in makes the frameworks harder to discard.
insights.quote: Business and human rights frameworks are not ‘Western’.
insights.locator: Business and human rights frameworks are not

insights.claim: Reported abuses involving Western companies show that the West does not have the competitive advantage it believes it has on ethical and responsible business practices.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Do not assign a governance premium to Western-domiciled miners by default; incident records, not domicile, should drive the risk assessment.
insights.quote: Reported abuses against Western companies show that the West does not have the competitive advantage that it thinks it has on ethical and responsible business practices.
insights.locator: Reported abuses against Western companies

insights.claim: China's new Mineral Resources Law, the International Initiative for Sustainability in the Resource Sector, and accompanying responsible-performance guidelines signal increasing Chinese attention to responsible production, even if implementation is not yet stringent.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
entities: International Initiative for Sustainability in the Resource Sector
insights.so_what: Chinese operators adopting responsibility standards would erode a perceived Western differentiator and reshape competition for producer-state access.
insights.locator: The Chinese government's announcement of its new Mineral Resources Law

themes.theme: Producer states reclaim the standards toolkit

insights.claim: The decisive factor in whether companies uphold responsible performance is the buy-in of the political leadership of host countries, with government National Action Plans a fundamental prerequisite for human rights due diligence to become operational practice.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
entities: UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights
insights.so_what: Screen jurisdictions by whether a National Action Plan exists and is enforced; that is a better predictor of project stability than company-level policy.
insights.locator: Partnered implementation

insights.claim: The Voluntary Principles on Security and Human Rights and its multi-stakeholder governance Initiative have increasing membership from the governments of extractive-dependent economies such as the DRC and Mozambique.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
entities: Voluntary Principles on Security and Human Rights
insights.so_what: Producer-state accession shifts these standards from buyer-imposed conditions to host-country requirements, changing who sets the compliance bar.
insights.locator: Similarly, the Voluntary Principles on Security

insights.claim: The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and the principle of free and prior informed consent are too often acknowledged but not actually enacted, leaving a gap between stated policy and site-level practice.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
entities: UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
insights.so_what: The acknowledgement-versus-enactment gap is where project delays originate; verify consent processes on the ground before underwriting greenfield timelines.
insights.quote: The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and the principle of free and prior informed consent (FPIC) are too often acknowledged, but not enacted.
insights.locator: Of course, implementation is vital

insights.claim: The Democratic Republic of the Congo's revised mining code addresses most of the most important social and environmental risks, but its beneficial impact depends entirely on enforcement.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Regulatory text in the DRC is no longer the binding constraint; enforcement capacity is, and that is what determines cost and compliance burden for operators there.
insights.quote: the DRC’s revised mining code addresses most of the most important social and environmental risks, but the potential beneficial impact depends on enforcement
insights.locator: For example, the DRC's revised mining code

insights.claim: The UN Secretary General's Initiative on Critical Energy Transition Minerals shows producer nations pursuing universal standards and could serve as a global convenor to extend implementation.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
entities: UN Secretary General's Initiative on Critical Energy Transition Minerals
insights.so_what: A producer-led standards forum would set terms of access for buyers; monitor it as a venue where future minerals compliance rules are drafted.
insights.locator: The UN Secretary General's Initiative

insights.claim: The standards toolkit devised a quarter century ago to protect the developing world from the excesses of global extractive industries is now being picked up by producer countries themselves to defend against the impacts of great-power competition, inverting who wields responsible-business norms.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect responsibility standards to be asserted as leverage by resource-holding states, raising the cost of access for buyers who assumed these norms were fading.
insights.quote: A quarter century ago, these tools were devised to protect the developing world from the excesses of global extractive industries. Today, it is those countries who are now picking up these tools to defend themselves
